Student Rights and Responsibility A.
Students who intend to transfer must inform themselves of the transfer admission requirements, and the program and degree requirements of the institution to which they expect to transfer.

Delay in choosing a major and a senior institution, changing the major or senior institution, or in not following the course of study may affect the applicability of transfer credit.
B.
When a student transfers under the course-to-course option, the articulation/transfer agreement in place when that student initiates the second half of the associate degree program (31 credit hours or more) will be the agreement that governs course equivalencies for that student.
C.

When a student transfers under a program-to-program transfer agreement, the student is governed by the requirements in effect at the beginning of the academic year in which the student was officially matriculated into the program.
These requirements will remain in effect for that student for five years regardless of changes to individual course equivalencies.
D.
If a student is not satisfied with a college or university transfer decision, the student may first appeal at the college or university -level and then at the system-level.

Each appeal decision must include an explanation of the decision.

The appeals procedure must be available in the college/university student handbook, catalog and on the website. 3.

The student may request assistance from academic advisors or the transfer /articulation officer at the sending institution in preparing the appeal. 4.
If upon completion of the appeals process at the institutional-level, the issue is not resolved, further appeal may be made at the system-level.

If a student is not satisfied with the college or university transfer appeals decision, the student may submit a request to the senior academic officer at the Office of the Postsecondary Commissioner for a systems-level appeal to the Interinstitutional Articulation Transfer Committee. 1.

The committee will consider the materials submitted by the student and the institutions of higher education within thirty (30) days if possible and no more than forty- five (45) days from the receipt of the request for an appeal. 4.

Faculty Senate Executive Committee Bill #2025-2026-03 November 20, 2025 Faculty Senate Meeting Approved by CASC 6/16/25 Approved by FSEC10/1/25 Rationale: URI's “Second Grade Option' (UM S8.33.32; SGO hereafter) allows students at the beginning of their URI career to retake courses in which they received a C- or below.
When they do so, the original grade remains on their transcript but is not used in QPA calculations.
The only exception to this rule occurs when determining whether students are eligible to graduate with distinction (≥3.3 cum laude, ≥3.5 magna cum laude, ≥3.7 summa cum laude).
The QPA to determine eligibility for this honor is calculated using ALL courses taken at the university, including any repeated using the SGO, rather than the QPA printed on the student's transcript.
This results in some students who exercised the SGO being ineligible for honors despite having a suitable QPA. on their transcript.
The argument for the current approach is comparing two students with the same QPA, one of whom exercised their rights to a SGO and the other who did not, the latter student is more deserving of graduation with distinction than the former.

Put another way, students wishing to graduate with distinction should be held to a ‘higher standard' than the transcript-listed QPA.
Jack Humphrey, the registrar, notes, “My research regarding the history of including all courses alt tempted at the University dates back to the 70's.
There was a concern that by not counting all attempts, academic honors could be awarded on an unequal basis (those that utilized the 2nd grade option could be given the academic honors as students that did not have any courses that qualified for the 2nd grade option).

In addition, since the 2nd grade option is not mandatory, it could disenfranchise students who chose to not exercise the 2nd grade option who would have otherwise qualified for academic honors had they chosen to use the 2nd grade option at the start of their undergraduate academic career My concern if we were to eliminate calculating distinction without taking into account all course attempts would be that distinction at commencement would become less meaningful." There was also concern changing the current policy might affect students who, although initially dismissed from URI for poor grades, significantly improved their academic performance after being readmitted under the ^conditional read mission' program (UM $8.25.13 - 8.25.16). the policy might increase their chances of earning this distinction.
There are two arguments against the current approach.
First, both the SGO and conditional read mission program provide a measure of forgiveness for mistakes made early in a student's career; the same principle should apply to studcnts’ ability to graduate with distinction.

Second, many students logically assume that the transcript-listed QPA determines eligibility -- the fact that it does not is confusing and engenders hard feelings in soon-to-be-alumni.
We ask the Faculty Senate to consider eliminating the sentence in s8.22.40 *Distinction* that specifies the QPA for graduating with distinction is calculated using all courses attempted at URI.
Its deletion would mean that student eligibility for graduating cum/ magna/summa laude would by default be determined using the transcript-listed QPA.
This would eliminate student confusion over their eligibility and ensure that the forgiveness embodied in the SGO and conditional read mission policies applies throughout a student's time at the university.
